issues.legal_issue: The value of mineral output supplied from an owned mine to the owner’s manufacturing facilities may be included when determining the mine’s profits for a cess assessment, even when the output is not sold separately.
material_facts: The company owned both a colliery and iron and steel factories and workshops.
Most of the coal raised from the colliery was supplied to and used in the company’s factories and workshops; some coal was sold to outsiders.
The company claimed that no profit from the colliery could be assessed on coal used in its own factories because that coal was not sold.
issues.conclusion: The assessing authority could take into consideration the value of the coal supplied to the company’s factories and workshops when computing the colliery’s profits.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 6 and 72 of the Bengal Cess Act, 1880, cess could be assessed on the annual net profits of a mine. Following Tata Iron and Steel Co. Ltd. v. State of Bihar, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 199, where mining and manufacturing are parts of an integrated undertaking and the mine’s profit is embedded in the proceeds from the ultimate product, the profit attributable to the mine may be identified and assessed. The fact that the mined material is consumed in manufacturing rather than incorporated into the final product does not alter that principle; the comparable education-cess provisions were treated similarly.

predicates.mine_profit_cess_assessment: An authority is assessing cess by reference to the profits of a mine.
predicates.integrated_mining_and_manufacturing: The mine and the owner’s manufacturing operations form parts of an integrated undertaking whose ultimate products are sold.
predicates.mine_output_used_in_owner_facilities: The owner supplies output from the mine to its own manufacturing facilities for use there.

issues.definition: When a mine’s output is used in the owner’s integrated manufacturing undertaking, its value may be included in determining the mine’s profits for a cess assessment.

issues.legal_issue: A civil suit cannot be used to challenge the correctness of a mine-profit assessment’s computation when a self-contained statutory scheme provides remedies for that challenge and the aggrieved person did not pursue those remedies on that issue.
material_facts: The company challenged the valuation used to compute the colliery’s profits, including the use of the controlled rate for coal supplied to its factories.
The statutory scheme provided a process for objections to a valuation and an appeal, with the appellate decision being final.
The company did not raise its complaint about the mode of computation before the assessing authority and the appellate authority through the prescribed procedure.

The company’s complaint was about the interpretation and application of the computation provisions, rather than a claim that the authority had violated a provision of the Act or fundamental principles of judicial procedure.
issues.conclusion: The company could not raise its computation challenge in the civil suit; the civil courts had no jurisdiction to examine the correctness of the authorities’ computation of net profits in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 75 and 102 of the Bengal Cess Act, 1880 provided for valuation by the Collector, objections, an appeal, and finality of the appellate decision. A special statutory scheme that creates a liability and provides its own remedies for errors in enforcement must be followed rather than bypassed by suit. Under Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh, [1968] 3 S.C.R. 662, civil jurisdiction is excluded where statutory orders are final and an adequate remedy is provided. Collector of South Arcot v. Mask & Co., 67 I.A. 222, recognizes that exclusion is not readily inferred and that civil courts may still examine statutory noncompliance or failure to follow fundamental principles of judicial procedure; that exception did not apply because the complaint concerned computation and interpretation, not such a failure.

rule.if: mine_cess_assessment_proceeding and statutory_scheme_provides_objection_and_appeal_with_finality and computation_challenge_not_pursued_through_statutory_remedies and challenge_is_to_assessment_correctness and not alleged_statutory_noncompliance_or_fundamental_procedural_failure

predicates.mine_cess_assessment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an assessment of cess by reference to a mine’s profits.
predicates.statutory_scheme_provides_objection_and_: The governing scheme provides a process to object to the assessment and appeal, and makes the resulting decision final.
predicates.computation_challenge_not_pursued_throug: The taxpayer did not use the prescribed objection and appeal process to raise the particular complaint about computation.
predicates.challenge_is_to_assessment_correctness: The complaint concerns the correctness of the assessment’s computation rather than the validity of the governing law.
predicates.not_alleged_statutory_noncompliance_or_f: The taxpayer does not allege that the authority failed to comply with the statute or with fundamental principles of judicial procedure.

issues.definition: When a taxpayer in a mine-cess assessment does not use an available final statutory remedy for a computation complaint, and alleges neither statutory noncompliance nor fundamental procedural failure, a civil court cannot review the computation’s correctness.
